Must be taken with food (at least ~500 kcal) for adequate absorption
Use only if benefit justifies risk; neonatal EPS/withdrawal risk in 3rd trimester
No adjustment for oral; IM cyclodextrin vehicle - caution in renal impairment
Use with caution; lower exposure data limited

summary: Ziprasidone is an atypical antipsychotic used for schizophrenia and acute manic/mixed episodes of bipolar I disorder, with an intramuscular form for acute agitation. It carries a boxed warning of increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Its defining safety issue is dose-related QT prolongation, so it is contraindicated with other QT-prolonging drugs and in patients with relevant cardiac risk. It must be taken with food to be absorbed adequately.
indications: Monotherapy for the acute treatment of bipolar I manic or mixed episodes
Maintenance treatment of bipolar I disorder as an adjunct to lithium or valproate

dosage.d: Start 20 mg twice daily; adjust up to 80 mg twice daily
dosage.n: Dose changes at intervals of >=2 days; take with food; use lowest effective dose

dosage.d: Start 40 mg twice daily, increase to 60-80 mg twice daily on day 2
dosage.n: Subsequent dosing 40-80 mg twice daily by response/tolerability

dosage.d: Continue effective dose, generally 40-80 mg twice daily with food
10 mg IM every 2 hours, or 20 mg IM every 4 hours
dosage.n: Maximum 40 mg/day IM; usually up to 3 consecutive days

admin: Take oral capsules with food (a meal of at least about 500 kcal) - food roughly doubles absorption
Swallow capsules whole; do not open, crush, or chew
Titrate gradually and use the lowest effective dose
Correct hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia before and during therapy
For IM use, reconstitute as directed and give by intramuscular injection only
moa: Ziprasidone's antipsychotic activity is thought to arise from combined antagonism of dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT2A receptors. It is also an agonist at 5-HT1A and antagonist at 5-HT2C and 5-HT1D receptors, and it moderately inhibits reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine, which may contribute to mood and cognitive effects. Its receptor profile gives relatively low metabolic burden but a notable effect on cardiac repolarization (QT).

absolute: Known history of QT prolongation (including congenital long QT syndrome)
Concomitant use with other QT-prolonging drugs
Use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors, or within 14 days of stopping an MAOI
relative: Elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis (increased mortality - not approved)
monitor: Mental status (including suicidality) and movement disorders

preg: Use during pregnancy only if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. Neonates exposed in the third trimester are at risk of extrapyramidal and/or withdrawal symptoms after delivery; monitor the newborn.
lact: It is not known whether ziprasidone is excreted in human milk; because of potential serious effects in the infant, breastfeeding is generally not recommended during treatment.
renal: No dose adjustment is needed for the oral form in renal impairment. The intramuscular formulation contains a cyclodextrin excipient cleared by the kidney, so use it with caution in renal impairment.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; clearance may be reduced. Data in significant hepatic disease are limited.

major: Other QT-prolonging drugs (Class IA/III antiarrhythmics, certain antibiotics/antifungals, methadone, etc.) - contraindicated due to additive QT risk
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors - contraindicated (serotonin syndrome/hypertensive crisis)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., ketoconazole) modestly increase levels; carbamazepine (inducer) lowers levels
moderate: Other CNS depressants and alcohol (additive sedation)
interactions.food: Food is required for adequate absorption - take with a meal of at least ~500 kcal
interactions.alcohol: Avoid - additive central nervous system depression and impaired judgment
interactions.diagnostics: Monitor ECG (QTc), electrolytes, glucose, and lipids

serious: QT prolongation / risk of torsades de pointes
emergency: Torsades de pointes / syncope from arrhythmia
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, autonomic instability)

monitoring: Baseline and follow-up ECG (QTc) when cardiac risk factors are present
Serum potassium and magnesium (correct before and during therapy)
Weight, fasting glucose / HbA1c, and lipid profile
Movement disorders (EPS, tardive dyskinesia) and mental status including suicidality
Complete blood count if signs of infection or low neutrophils
counsel: Always take this medicine with food - it does not work well on an empty stomach
Do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you, and rise slowly to avoid dizziness
Seek urgent care for fainting, palpitations, irregular heartbeat, high fever with stiffness, or a painful erection lasting over 4 hours
Avoid alcohol and tell your doctor about all other medicines, especially for heart rhythm or depression (MAOIs)
Do not stop suddenly; report new or worsening mood or thoughts of self-harm
pk: Antipsychotic effect develops over days to weeks; IM agitation effect within ~1 hour
Oral peak ~6-8 hours (with food); IM peak ~60 minutes
Oral about 7 hours; IM about 2-5 hours
Store capsules at 15-30 C; reconstituted IM solution per labeling (protect from light)
pearls: BOXED WARNING: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis - not approved for this use
Dose-related QT prolongation is the hallmark risk - contraindicated with other QT-prolonging drugs and in relevant cardiac disease; correct K+ and Mg2+
Absorption roughly doubles with food - always dose with a meal of at least ~500 kcal
Generally lower metabolic (weight/glucose/lipid) burden than some other atypicals, but still monitor
missed: Take the missed dose with food as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and take the next dose with food as usual - do not double up.
overdose: Overdose may cause sedation, slurred speech, hypertension, extrapyramidal symptoms, and, importantly, QT prolongation with risk of arrhythmia. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive with airway protection, continuous cardiac (ECG) monitoring for arrhythmia, and correction of electrolytes; ziprasidone is highly protein bound, so dialysis is unlikely to help.
